name: Helvetica
fact: It launched as "Neue Haas Grotesk" and was renamed in 1960 to Helvetica, from the Latin name for Switzerland, to sell better abroad.

name: Tiempos
fact: It grew out of a newspaper redesign project and became a staple of editorial design.

name: Klavika
fact: Facebook's original wordmark was based on Klavika.

name: Iowan Old Style
fact: Downer, also a sign painter, drew it. It later became one of the reading fonts in Apple Books.

name: Stencil
fact: Two different typefaces called "Stencil" were released within months of each other in 1937, one by ATF and one by Ludlow.

name: Glypha
fact: It is a lighter, tighter take on Serifa with a larger x-height.

name: Comic Sans
fact: Connare based it on the lettering in comic books he had at his desk. It was made for Microsoft Bob's speech bubbles but finished too late to ship with Bob.

name: Raleway
fact: It started as a single thin weight and was later expanded by the community into a full family.

name: New York
fact: Kare's original New York was the Mac's serif. In 2019 Apple reused the name for a new serif family.

name: Retina
fact: It was made for The Wall Street Journal's stock listings and printed at tiny sizes (about 5.5 points) on newsprint.

name: Tiresias
designer: Royal National Institute of Blind People
fact: It is named after the blind prophet of Greek mythology and was designed for subtitles and signage readable by people with low vision.

name: Josefin Sans
fact: It was inspired by geometric Swedish designs of the 1920s.

name: Cormorant
fact: It is a free, very high-contrast take on Garamond, designed to look elegant at huge sizes.

name: GT Walsheim
fact: It was inspired by poster lettering by the Swiss designer Otto Baumberger.

name: Cooper Black
fact: That chunky title on the Beach Boys' album Pet Sounds is Cooper Black. The typeface became shorthand for 1970s warmth.

name: Bodoni
fact: Bodoni's "Manuale Tipografico", showcasing hundreds of typefaces, was published by his widow in 1818, five years after he died.

name: Lobster
fact: This free, bold script became so common online in the early 2010s that designers begged each other to stop using it.

name: Silkscreen
fact: It was designed for tiny text on websites in the Flash era, when pixel fonts stayed crisp.

name: FE-Schrift
fact: It is used on German license plates and designed to be hard to tamper with. You can't easily paint a P into an R or an E into a B.

name: Guardian Egyptian
fact: It was made for The Guardian's 2005 redesign and grew into a huge family for everything from headlines to body text.

name: Tw Cen MT
fact: It is a digital descendant of Sol Hess's Twentieth Century and ships with Office.

name: Avenir
fact: "Avenir" is French for "future," a nod to Futura. Frutiger wanted a warmer, more human geometric sans.

name: Broadway
fact: Its dramatic thick-and-thin letters became the typeface of the Jazz Age.

name: Computer Modern
fact: Knuth made it with his own METAFONT program, and it became the default look of TeX and LaTeX papers.

name: PT Sans
fact: It was made to mark 300 years since Peter the Great's reform of the Cyrillic alphabet and is free to use.

name: Wilhelm Klingspor Gotisch
fact: It was named in memory of Wilhelm Klingspor of the Klingspor type-foundry family and is considered one of the finest 20th-century blackletters.

name: Westminster
fact: It borrows the chunky look of cheque MICR digits and became the go-to "computer" font of the 1960s and 70s.

name: Hobo
fact: Its letters have almost no straight lines, and it has no true descenders. The name's origin is still a mystery.

name: Edwardian Script
fact: It captures pointed-pen copperplate writing and was one of Benguiat's many scripts.

name: Nimbus Sans
fact: URW's Helvetica clone ships with Ghostscript, so it quietly stands in for Helvetica on countless Linux systems.

name: Bulmer
fact: It was cut for William Bulmer's Shakespeare Printing Office to print the Boydell edition of Shakespeare.

name: SF Mono
fact: It is the monospaced cousin of San Francisco, used in Xcode and Terminal.

name: Palatino
fact: It is named after Giambattista Palatino, a 16th-century Italian master of handwriting.

name: Coronet
fact: Its light, bouncy look defined a lot of mid-century American packaging.

name: Graphik
fact: It was designed as a plain, modern grotesque and became common in magazines and tech branding.

name: Roboto
fact: It debuted with Android 4.0 "Ice Cream Sandwich" and became Android's signature font.

name: Gill Sans Ultra Bold
fact: Nicknamed "Kayo" (knockout), it is so heavy it barely resembles Gill Sans.

name: Spectral
fact: It was designed by Production Type and released with Google for elegant reading on screens.

name: Garamond Premier
fact: Slimbach went back to Garamond's original punches for this, one of the most historically faithful Garamonds.

name: FF Trixie
fact: It is reportedly based on the worn type of an old typewriter belonging to a friend named Beatrix.

name: ITC Benguiat
fact: The glowing red Stranger Things title is set in Benguiat, which pulled the typeface back into pop culture.

name: Octavian
fact: Two British letter-cutters made it, and it shows the influence of stone lettering.

name: Joanna
fact: Gill named it after his daughter Joanna and used it to set his own "An Essay on Typography."

name: Chaparral
fact: It blends 19th-century slab lettering with Renaissance book-hand proportions.

name: Kabel
fact: The name is German for "cable" and reportedly honours a new telecommunications cable of the day. Its slanted strokes make it unusually lively for a geometric sans.

name: Consolas
fact: Microsoft made it for coders, and it was tuned for ClearType screen rendering.

name: Cantarell
fact: It became the default interface font of the GNOME desktop.

name: Bookerly
fact: Amazon commissioned it as the Kindle's own reading font, replacing Caecilia as the default.

name: Ubuntu
fact: The Ubuntu Linux distribution commissioned it as its interface and brand font.

name: Janson
fact: For years it was credited to the Dutch printer Anton Janson. Scholars later traced it to Kis, a Hungarian punchcutter.

name: Template Gothic
fact: Deck based it on stencil lettering he saw on a sign at a laundromat. It came to define 1990s grunge design.

name: FF DIN
fact: Pool refined the German DIN 1451 standard into a family designers could use for text.

name: Mrs Eaves
fact: It is named after Sarah Eaves, John Baskerville's housekeeper, who became his wife and ran the business after he died.

name: Benton Sans
fact: It is a revival of Morris Fuller Benton's News Gothic, named in his honour.

name: Bank Gothic
fact: Its squared-off capitals give it a technological look, and science-fiction titles love it.

name: Brandon Grotesque
fact: It is influenced by the geometric sans serifs of the 1920s and 30s, with a slightly softer finish.

name: Montserrat
fact: It was inspired by old posters and signage in the Montserrat neighbourhood of Buenos Aires.

name: ITC Avant Garde Gothic
fact: It grew out of the logo for Avant Garde magazine. Its many tight ligatures were so often misused that designers joked about banning them.

name: Source Han Sans
fact: Each font has 65,535 glyphs, the maximum an OpenType font can hold, to cover Chinese, Japanese and Korean.

name: Lutetia
fact: "Lutetia" is the Latin name for Paris. The face was shown at the 1925 Paris Exposition.

name: Twentieth Century
fact: This Monotype design was the basis for Century Gothic.

name: Source Sans Pro
fact: It was Adobe's first open-source typeface family.

name: Snell Roundhand
fact: It is based on the flowing penmanship of 17th-century English writing master Charles Snell.

name: Egyptienne F
fact: It was one of the first typefaces designed specifically for phototypesetting.

name: Hypatia Sans
fact: It is named after Hypatia of Alexandria, the ancient philosopher and mathematician.

name: Johnston100
fact: It marked Johnston's 100th birthday with new weights for Transport for London.

name: Helvetica Neue
fact: This reworked Helvetica borrowed Univers' numbered weight system, so "Helvetica 55" became as familiar as "Univers 55."

name: Bell Centennial
fact: It was made for AT&T phone books. Its "ink traps" (notches cut into corners) kept letters sharp on cheap paper at tiny sizes.

name: FF Meta
fact: It began as a font for the German Post Office, which never used it. Later it was nicknamed "the Helvetica of the '90s."

name: Zapf Dingbats
fact: It was one of the 35 fonts built into PostScript printers, so almost every laser printer could print its stars, checks and pointing hands.

name: Fournier
fact: Fournier published an early typographic point system in 1737, an ancestor of how we measure type today.

name: Excelsior
fact: It was part of Linotype's "Legibility Group," designed to stay readable on fast presses and cheap newsprint.

name: Antique Olive
fact: Its tall x-height and quirky, thick-topped letters gave French design a distinctive voice, including the Air France logo.

name: Bradley Hand
fact: It is based on the designer's own handwriting and ships with Windows and macOS.

name: Diotima
fact: Zapf-von Hesse was one of the few prominent women type designers of her generation. Diotima is named after a wise woman in Plato's Symposium.

name: Optima
fact: Zapf got the idea from inscriptions in the floor of Santa Croce in Florence and made his first sketches on a 1,000-lira banknote.

name: Fira Sans
fact: It was designed for Mozilla's Firefox OS and released free for anyone to use.

name: Folio
fact: It came out in 1957, the same year as Helvetica and Univers, and lost the popularity race to both.

name: Electra
fact: Dwiggins aimed for a book face with "warmth and personality." Unusually, its italic started out as a sloped roman.

name: Caledonia
fact: Dwiggins is credited with coining the term "graphic designer" in 1922.

name: Erbar
fact: Erbar started work on it in 1922, which makes it one of the earliest geometric sans serifs, ahead of Futura.

name: Minion
fact: It is named after "minion," a traditional name for a small type size (around 7 points).

name: DejaVu Sans
fact: It extended Bitstream Vera with thousands of extra characters and became a Linux default.

name: Merriweather
fact: It was designed for comfortable reading on screens and became one of Google Fonts' most-used serifs.

name: Tahoma
fact: It is a close relative of Verdana with tighter spacing and was the Windows interface font for years.

name: Plantin
fact: It is named after the 16th-century Antwerp printer Christophe Plantin and was one of the models for Times New Roman.

name: Castellar
fact: Its engraved-looking Roman capitals come across as formal and ceremonial.

name: Neuland
fact: Koch cut the punches directly in metal without drawings first, so every size came out slightly different. The Jurassic Park logo made it famous again.

name: Century Gothic
fact: A U.S. university once switched its default font to Century Gothic because it reportedly used less printer ink than Arial.

name: Wingdings
fact: Microsoft built it from Bigelow & Holmes' symbol designs. A long-running hoax claimed typing "NYC" in it hid a secret message.

name: Archer
fact: It was first made for Martha Stewart Living. Its round ball terminals give it a friendly, crafty feel.

name: Schwabacher
fact: This round, lively blackletter was the everyday type of Luther-era German printing.

name: Bembo
fact: It is named after the poet Pietro Bembo, whose short book "De Aetna" was the first thing printed in this roman type by Aldus Manutius.

name: Literata
fact: It was commissioned for Google Play Books and designed for long reading on screens.

name: Hoefler Text
fact: Apple commissioned it, and it shipped with the Mac to show off advanced typography features.

name: Memphis
fact: It is one of the first geometric slab serifs: basically Futura with slabs.

name: Playfair Display
fact: It is inspired by the high-contrast letters of the late 18th century, when pointed-pen writing influenced type.

name: Parisine
fact: It is the signage typeface of the Paris Métro, drawn to be clear in underground lighting.

name: Akzidenz-Grotesk
fact: This workhorse of Swiss modernism was the direct inspiration for both Helvetica and Univers.

name: Latin Modern
fact: It extends Knuth's Computer Modern with many more accented characters.

name: OCR-A
fact: It was designed for early optical scanners. Its odd shapes were easy for machines to read, and they became a retro-futurist style.

name: Work Sans
fact: It was loosely inspired by early grotesques such as those in Stephenson Blake specimens.

name: Charcoal
fact: It replaced Chicago as the system font in Mac OS 8.

name: Beowolf
designer: Erik van Blokland & Just van Rossum
fact: Using PostScript tricks, its letter outlines randomly change each time you print, so no two copies look exactly the same.

name: Monaco
fact: Monaco was the Mac's default terminal font for years before Menlo took over.

name: Century Schoolbook
fact: Benton designed it for textbooks after research on legibility for young readers. The U.S. Supreme Court requires briefs in the Century family.

name: San Francisco (2015)
fact: Apple's system font debuted on the Apple Watch before spreading to iPhone and Mac.

name: Webdings
fact: It was designed so web pages could use pictograms before emoji existed, when an icon meant an image download.

name: Hiragino
fact: It has been the main Japanese typeface on Macs and iPhones for years.

name: Bell
fact: It was cut for John Bell's British Letter Foundry and is considered one of the first English "modern" faces.

name: Dead History
fact: Makela spliced together parts of two existing typefaces, VAG Rounded and Centennial Script, to make one hybrid.

name: Alternate Gothic
fact: It came in three widths so printers could fit headlines of different lengths. That need gave it a very long life.

name: Transport
fact: It is the lettering on British road signs. Calvert also drew many of the UK's road-sign pictograms, such as the "children crossing" sign.

name: Verlag
fact: It began as the typeface for the Guggenheim Museum's identity.

name: Narkis
fact: Narkiss designed many Hebrew faces, including lettering for Israeli banknotes and stamps.

name: Centaur
fact: Rogers based it on Nicolas Jenson's 15th-century roman and first drew it for the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

name: Cooper Hewitt
fact: The Smithsonian Design Museum released its typeface as open source, which was unusual for a museum identity.

name: Georgia
fact: Carter designed it for screens at Microsoft. The name reportedly comes from a tabloid headline, "Alien Heads Found in Georgia."

name: Mason
fact: It was originally named "Manson." After complaints, the publisher shortened the name to Mason.

name: ITC Souvenir
designer: Morris Fuller Benton (ITC revival by Ed Benguiat)
fact: It was barely used after 1914, then Benguiat's 1970 ITC revival made it one of the defining looks of the 1970s.

name: Product Sans
fact: Google created it for its 2015 logo redesign. Its "G" became one of the most seen letters on Earth.

name: Bookman
fact: It started as "Old Style Antique" and got the name Bookman later. Its wide, sturdy letters survive rough printing.

name: Utopia
fact: Adobe later donated a version to TeX users, so it often turns up in academic papers.

name: Vectora
fact: Frutiger based it on American gothics such as Franklin Gothic and News Gothic.

name: Aldine Italic
fact: This was the first italic type. Aldus Manutius used it to fit more text into small, affordable pocket editions.

name: New Alphabet
fact: Crouwel built it only from horizontal and vertical lines for early screens. It was so radical that many letters are hard to read.

name: Open Sans
fact: It was one of the first big free fonts on Google Fonts and was served billions of times across the web.

name: Trajan
fact: It is based on the inscription at the base of Trajan's Column in Rome (113 AD) and has capitals only. It became a fixture of movie posters.

name: Textura (Gutenberg B42)
fact: The type for Gutenberg's Bible had about 290 different sorts (ligatures, abbreviations, variant letters) to imitate a scribe's hand.

name: VAG Rounded
fact: It was made for Volkswagen, hence "VAG," and later spread far beyond cars, including to keyboards and signage.

name: Friz Quadrata
fact: Friz began it, and Victor Caruso of ITC completed the family. Its chiselled letters lean between serif and sans.

name: Ondine
fact: Frutiger drew it from lettering cut with scissors and a broad-pen feel.

name: Calvert
fact: The Tyne and Wear Metro in Newcastle used it for decades.

name: Sabon
fact: It was commissioned to look identical whether set by hand, on Linotype machines or on Monotype machines, a tough constraint at the time.

name: American Typewriter
fact: Milton Glaser set the famous "I ♥ NY" logo in American Typewriter.

name: Thesis (TheSans)
fact: It was one of the largest type families ever, with sans, serif, mono and more in many weights.

name: Fell Types
fact: Bishop John Fell gave Oxford University Press a collection of type he had bought from the Netherlands. Its digital revival is free.

name: Doves Type
fact: After a feud with his partner, Cobden-Sanderson threw all the metal type off a London bridge into the Thames. Divers recovered some of it in 2015.

name: Bickham Script
fact: It is based on engravings from George Bickham's 18th-century penmanship book "The Universal Penman."

name: Gill Sans
fact: It was adopted by the London and North Eastern Railway and later became the face of Penguin Books covers and the BBC's logo.

name: Mona Sans
fact: GitHub named it after its Octocat mascot, Mona, and released it free.

name: Operator
fact: This coding font pairs a monospaced roman with a cursive, handwriting-like italic.

name: City
fact: Paul Rand's 1956 IBM logo was based on City Medium.

name: American Uncial
fact: Hammer was inspired by early medieval Irish manuscripts such as the Book of Kells.

name: Fedra Sans
fact: It began as a corporate typeface that was never used, then was released commercially and grew to cover many scripts.

name: Noto
fact: The name means "no tofu." "Tofu" is slang for the blank boxes shown when a font lacks a character, and Noto aims to cover every script in Unicode.

name: Bell Gothic
fact: It was the phone-book typeface before Bell Centennial replaced it in the 1970s.

name: Akkurat
fact: This sharp Swiss grotesque became a favourite of art-world and museum identities.

name: Agency FB
fact: It began as a caps-only face, and Font Bureau later expanded it into a full family.

name: Park Avenue
fact: This Art Deco-era script was a favourite for elegant menus and ads.

name: Fette Fraktur
fact: In 1941 the Nazi regime abruptly banned blackletter type, falsely calling it "Jewish letters," and ordered a switch to roman type.

name: Exocet
fact: Its rough, ancient-inscription look made it the typeface of the Diablo video game series.

name: Geneva
fact: One of the original Mac fonts, it was a small-screen take on Helvetica.

name: Old English Text
fact: It is the blackletter many people meet first. It ships with Windows and shows up on diplomas and tattoos.

name: Eurostile
fact: Its rounded-rectangle shapes echo 1960s TV screens, which is why it keeps turning up in science fiction.

name: Space Mono
fact: Colophon designed it for Google with a retro-futuristic editorial feel.

name: Barlow
fact: It was inspired by California highway signs and license plates.

name: Peignot
fact: Cassandre mixed upper- and lowercase shapes in one alphabet, trying to reform the Latin alphabet itself.

name: Proxima Nova
fact: It began in 1994 as the smaller Proxima Sans and grew into one of the most popular web fonts of the 2010s.

name: Motter Tektura
fact: Apple used this jaunty face in the late 1970s, and Reebok used it in its logo.

name: Arno
fact: It is named after the Arno, the river that runs through Florence, where the Italian Renaissance types that inspired it were made.

name: Comic Neue
fact: A deliberate "grown-up" redesign of Comic Sans that keeps the friendliness and drops the awkwardness.

name: Univers
fact: Frutiger named its weights with numbers instead of words. "55" is roman, the tens digit sets the weight and the ones digit sets the width.

name: Inter
fact: Andersson designed it for computer screens, with a tall x-height for small UI text.

name: Lato
fact: "Lato" means "summer" in Polish. It was designed to feel warm and stable at text sizes and sleek in headlines.

name: Verdana
fact: When IKEA switched from Futura to Verdana in 2009, the backlash was big enough that the press called it "Verdanagate."

name: Franklin Gothic
fact: It is named after Benjamin Franklin, who was a printer before he was a founding father.

name: Alegreya
fact: It was designed for literature and has a lively, calligraphic rhythm for long reading.

name: Rockwell
fact: Slab serifs were once called "Egyptians," a name from the craze for all things Egyptian after Napoleon's campaign there.

name: Imprint
fact: It was one of the first typefaces designed for mechanical typesetting on Monotype machines, and was made for The Imprint journal.

name: Neutraface
fact: It is based on the lettering on buildings by the modernist architect Richard Neutra.

name: Copperplate Gothic
fact: It has no lowercase. Its tiny, crisp serifs imitate engraving and have made it a classic on business cards.

name: Geist
fact: Vercel designed it for developers and released it free alongside a mono version.

name: Highway Gothic
fact: This is the lettering on most U.S. road signs. It was drawn for legibility at speed, not for beauty.

name: Circular
fact: This Swiss geometric sans became the voice of many tech brands. Spotify used it for years.

name: Corona
fact: It became one of the most widely used U.S. newspaper text faces of the mid-20th century.

name: Lubalin Graph
fact: It adds slab serifs to the geometric skeleton of ITC Avant Garde.

name: Bifur
fact: Each letter keeps only its most distinctive part, with the rest suggested by fine lines, making it one of the boldest Art Deco experiments.

name: Grotesque (Caslon Egyptian)
fact: Caslon IV's "Two Lines English Egyptian" is considered the first sans-serif typeface. It had capitals only, and few people used it at first.

name: Eckmann
fact: Eckmann, a painter, brought flowing Jugendstil plant forms into type.

name: DIN 1451
fact: It was created as a German industrial standard for signage, engineering drawings and license plates. Designers later adopted it as a style icon.

name: Bernhard Fashion
fact: Its very light, elegant letters captured the fashion ads of the late 1920s.

name: Liberation
fact: Red Hat commissioned it to be metric-compatible with Arial, Times New Roman and Courier New, so documents keep the same layout on Linux.

name: Surveyor
fact: It is inspired by the lettering on 19th-century maps and engraved charts.

name: Trade Gothic
fact: Burke kept adding weights and widths over many years. Its condensed bold versions are a newsroom and sportswear staple.

name: Kepler
fact: It is named after the astronomer Johannes Kepler.

name: Oswald
fact: It reworks the classic Alternate Gothic style for screens.

name: Serifa
fact: Frutiger built it from the skeleton of his own Univers and added slab serifs.

name: Clarendon
fact: It was one of the first typefaces registered under Britain's Ornamental Designs Act of 1842. The protection lasted only three years before copies appeared.

name: Rubik
fact: It was designed for Google's Chrome Cube Lab, a project celebrating the Rubik's Cube.

name: Cairo
fact: This Mac picture font is where Clarus the Dogcow comes from, the mascot of Mac page-setup dialogs.

name: Trebuchet MS
fact: It is named after the medieval siege engine. Connare liked the idea of a font that could "launch" text across the internet.

name: Arnold Böcklin
fact: It is named after the Swiss Symbolist painter Arnold Böcklin and is quintessential Art Nouveau.

name: Myriad
fact: Apple used Myriad as its corporate typeface for over a decade, including on early iPod ads.

name: ITC Officina
fact: It was designed for office correspondence printed on low-quality laser printers.

name: Monaspace
fact: It uses "texture healing," which lets wide letters borrow space from narrow neighbours, evening out monospaced text.

name: Swiss 721
fact: Bitstream sold Helvetica under a code name. Swiss 721 is Helvetica, and "Dutch 801" is their Times.

name: Pacifico
fact: It channels 1950s American surf culture and its signs.

name: Marker Felt
fact: It looks like felt-tip marker. It's the font behind the early iPhone Notes app's yellow-paper look.

name: ITC Serif Gothic
fact: Its tiny serifs on a sans structure made it popular for 1970s album and movie titles.

name: EB Garamond
fact: It is a free revival based on a 1592 type specimen by the Egenolff-Berner foundry that showed Garamond's type.

name: ITC Bauhaus
fact: It was based on Herbert Bayer's 1925 "universal" alphabet. Bayer argued for dropping capital letters entirely.

name: New York (2019)
fact: Apple's modern serif takes its name from Susan Kare's 1984 bitmap font.

name: Karmina
fact: Burian and Scaglione co-founded TypeTogether, a foundry focused on text typefaces.

name: IBM Plex
fact: Plex replaced Helvetica Neue as IBM's corporate typeface, and IBM released it as open source.

name: Space Grotesk
fact: It was derived from Space Mono, a retro-futurist monospaced font by Colophon.

name: Jokerman
fact: Its busy dots and swirls made it a fixture of 1990s school projects.

name: Vollkorn
fact: "Vollkorn" means "wholegrain" in German. Althausen wanted a hearty, everyday bread-and-butter text face.

name: Aldus
fact: It is named after Aldus Manutius and was made as a lighter text companion to Palatino.

name: Imperial
fact: The New York Times used Imperial for its body text for decades.

name: Karnak
fact: It is named after the Karnak temple complex in Egypt, keeping up the "Egyptian" slab-serif naming habit.

name: Frutiger
fact: It began as the signage typeface for Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris, where it had to be readable at a distance and at an angle.

name: Walbaum
fact: Walbaum ran a foundry in Weimar. His crisp modern faces are a German counterpart to Bodoni and Didot.

name: Calibri
fact: It replaced Times New Roman as Microsoft Office's default in 2007 and held that spot until Aptos took over in 2023.

name: E-13B (MICR)
fact: The strange numbers at the bottom of cheques are printed in magnetic ink, and each shape has a unique magnetic signature for bank machines.

name: News Gothic
fact: The Star Wars opening crawl is commonly identified as News Gothic.

name: Wallau
fact: It is named after Heinrich Wallau, a respected German printer and scholar.

name: Letter Gothic
fact: It was designed for IBM electric typewriters and later became a favourite for code and technical documents.

name: Chicago
fact: The original Macintosh system font. Steve Jobs wanted the Mac's fonts named after world-class cities, so Kare's set included Geneva, New York and Monaco.

name: Scotch Roman
fact: This Scottish type found huge success in the United States, where it became a classic book and newspaper face.

name: Garage Gothic
fact: It is based on the numbers printed on parking-garage tickets.

name: Arial Black
fact: The ultra-heavy Arial shipped with Microsoft's core web fonts.

name: Corbel
fact: It was part of Microsoft's ClearType font collection and tuned for LCD screens.

name: Garamond
fact: Many typefaces sold as "Garamond" are actually based on type cut by Jean Jannon around 1615, and were misattributed to Garamond for centuries.

name: Gotham
fact: It was drawn for GQ magazine from mid-century lettering on New York buildings. The 2008 Obama campaign made it famous.

name: Baskerville
fact: Baskerville was obsessive about quality. To show off his type he helped develop smoother "wove" paper and a glossier black ink.

name: Meiryo
fact: Its name comes from Japanese meaning "clear" or "lucid." It was designed for readable Japanese on screens.

name: Zapfino
fact: Type the word "Zapfino" in the font and the letters join into one elaborate ligature, a hidden signature built into the font.

name: Bitstream Vera
fact: Bitstream released it under a free licence for GNOME. It spawned DejaVu and eventually Apple's Menlo.

name: Founders Grotesk
fact: It is based on classic British grotesques from the Miller & Richard foundry.

name: Brush Script
fact: It looks like fast brush lettering and was once shorthand for mid-century diners, signs and ads.

name: Rotis
fact: It is named after Rotis, the small German hamlet where Aicher lived and worked. He also designed the 1972 Munich Olympics pictograms.

name: Arial
fact: Every Arial character is exactly as wide as its Helvetica counterpart, so documents could swap one for the other without reflowing.

name: FF Scala
fact: It was designed for the Vredenburg music centre in Utrecht and named in honour of Milan's Teatro alla Scala.

name: Adobe Garamond
fact: Slimbach studied original 16th-century Garamond type at the Plantin-Moretus Museum in Antwerp.

name: Spectrum
fact: It was designed for a Bible from the Dutch publisher Het Spectrum, which gave it its name.

name: Albertus
fact: You'll see it on City of London street signs and in the opening titles of the cult 1960s TV series The Prisoner.

name: Caecilia
fact: For years this friendly slab serif was the default reading font on Amazon Kindles.

name: Recursive
fact: One variable font slides from a monospaced coding style to a casual, brushy style.

name: Andale Mono
fact: It was one of Microsoft's "Core fonts for the Web" and was built for clear code.

name: Schneidler
fact: Schneidler was an influential teacher in Stuttgart. His students included Georg Trump and Imre Reiner.

name: Avenir Next
fact: Frutiger worked with Akira Kobayashi to expand Avenir with more weights and widths, and it became a staple of Apple's system fonts.

name: JetBrains Mono
fact: It uses a taller x-height than most coding fonts to make code easier to read at small sizes.

name: Dante
fact: Punchcutter Charles Malin cut it by hand. It was first used for an edition of Boccaccio's life of Dante.

name: Weiss
fact: Weiss was a painter and poet as well as a type designer, and it shows in the typeface's delicate calligraphic feel.

name: Cambria
fact: Its companion Cambria Math is one of the most complete fonts for mathematical notation.

name: Mallory
fact: It combines British and American type traditions. It was Frere-Jones's first release from his own foundry.

name: Adobe Caslon
fact: Twombly based it on Caslon's own specimen sheets from the 1730s–1760s.

name: Söhne
fact: Klim describes it as "the memory of Akzidenz-Grotesk framed through the Helvetica of the New York subway."

name: Shelley
fact: It is a formal English roundhand script for invitations and certificates.

name: Baby Teeth
fact: Glaser based it on a hand-painted sign he saw in Mexico City.

name: League Gothic
fact: A free, open-source revival of Alternate Gothic from a group that set out to make quality free fonts.

name: Galliard
fact: It is based on the work of 16th-century punchcutter Robert Granjon and named after a lively Renaissance dance.

name: Sentinel
fact: Hoefler & Co. designed it as a slab serif with a true italic, which slab serifs had long lacked.

name: Playbill
fact: Its reversed-stress look (thick horizontals, thin verticals) instantly says "Wild West wanted poster."

name: Cloister Black
designer: Morris Fuller Benton & Joseph W. Phinney
fact: This classic blackletter became the default for "Old English" newspaper mastheads and certificates.

name: Druk
fact: Its ultra-heavy, ultra-condensed styles are made for giant headlines.

name: Gentium
fact: It was created for SIL International to support the huge range of Latin, Greek and Cyrillic characters used in minority languages.

name: Filosofia
fact: Licko's personal take on Bodoni, with softened contrast so it holds up at text sizes.

name: Didot
fact: The Didot family also gave its name to the Didot point, a unit of type measurement still used in parts of Europe.

name: Poliphilus
fact: It was used to print the "Hypnerotomachia Poliphili," often called the most beautiful book of the Renaissance.

name: Netflix Sans
fact: Netflix commissioned its own typeface, reportedly partly to save on font licensing fees.

name: AMS Euler
fact: Zapf designed it with Donald Knuth for the American Mathematical Society. It gives math an upright, handwritten feel.

name: Amiri
fact: It is a free revival of the elegant Naskh type used by Cairo's Bulaq Press in the early 20th century.

name: Charlemagne
fact: It is based on the capitals of Carolingian manuscripts from the era of Charlemagne.

name: Bebas Neue
fact: It started as a free all-caps display font and became one of the most-used headline fonts on the web.

name: Algerian
fact: Once a Victorian-style decorative face, it became a familiar option in word-processor font menus.

name: Nanum Gothic
fact: Naver released the Nanum fonts for free, and they became some of the most common Korean fonts on the web.

name: Chalkboard
fact: Mac users met it as a "chalk on a blackboard" style font bundled with the system.

name: Mistral
fact: In metal type its letters connect so smoothly that it looks truly handwritten, which was quite a technical feat for the time.

name: Papyrus
fact: Costello was 23 when he drew it by hand over roughly six months. Decades later it starred in an SNL sketch about the Avatar logo.

name: Johnston
fact: Commissioned for the London Underground, it has been in use for over a century. Its modern descendant, New Johnston, still appears on Tube signs.

name: Whitney
fact: It was designed for the Whitney Museum in New York and had to work on both signage and print.

name: Syntax
fact: Meier based it on Renaissance roman letterforms, giving a sans serif the rhythm of a book face.

name: Haettenschweiler
fact: This ultra-condensed face shipped with Windows, so plenty of people know the name without knowing where it came from.

name: Golden Type
fact: Morris designed it for his Kelmscott Press as part of his revolt against the poor quality of Victorian printing.

name: Quicksand
fact: This rounded display face was later expanded into a full free family on Google Fonts.

name: Lydian
fact: Chappell drew it with a broad pen, which gives a sans serif an elegant thick-and-thin rhythm.

name: BBC Reith
fact: It is named after Lord Reith, the BBC's founding director general.

name: Atkinson Hyperlegible
fact: It was made for low-vision readers, with letters that are hard to confuse, like I, l and 1. It is named after Braille Institute founder J. Robert Atkinson.

name: Bernhard Modern
fact: Bernhard, a poster pioneer, is famous for the "Sachplakat" (object poster) style.

name: Poetica
fact: It has an enormous set of alternate letters and swashes, so no two words need look the same.

name: DM Sans
fact: It was developed from Poppins as a low-contrast sans for small text.

name: Constantia
fact: It is the ClearType collection's book serif, designed to be readable both on screen and in print.

name: Nofret
fact: It is named after Nefertiti, the Egyptian queen.

name: OCR-B
fact: This friendlier machine-readable font is still used for the numbers under barcodes and the machine-readable zone of passports.

name: Segoe UI
fact: It has been the core of Windows' interface since Windows Vista.

name: Frank Rühl
fact: It is one of the most widely used Hebrew text typefaces, especially in books and newspapers.

name: Book Antiqua
fact: Hermann Zapf strongly objected to this Palatino lookalike, which shipped with Microsoft Office.

name: Hershey Fonts
fact: Hershey made them at the U.S. Naval Weapons Laboratory as stroke-based letters for early computer plotters.

name: Kennerley
fact: It was designed for publisher Mitchell Kennerley. Its success helped launch Goudy's career.

name: ITC Kabel
designer: Rudolf Koch (ITC revival by Victor Caruso)
fact: ITC's 1976 version enlarged the x-height, giving Kabel a very different disco-era feel.

name: Cascadia Code
fact: It launched with the new Windows Terminal and was named after the Cascadia region where Microsoft is based.

name: Courier
fact: Kettler drew it for IBM typewriters. He said "a letter can be just an ordinary letter, or it can be a courier" and picked the dignified name.

name: Mandatory
fact: This is the typeface legally required on UK number plates since 2001, which ended a free-for-all of decorative plates.

name: Didot HTF
fact: It was made for Harper's Bazaar in sizes cut for different scales, so hairlines stay sharp even when huge.

name: Arnhem
fact: It was originally designed for the Nederlandse Staatscourant, the Dutch government gazette.

name: Obsidian
fact: It uses computer-generated 3D lighting on engraved letters to imitate 19th-century decorative type.

name: Iosevka
fact: It is narrow, so you can fit more code side by side. Users can build their own custom versions from its source code.

name: ITC Tiffany
fact: It combines features of Ronaldson and Caxton Old Style, with Art Nouveau flair.

name: Noori Nastaliq
fact: Nastaliq's slanting cascades are notoriously hard to typeset. Jamil's system used thousands of pre-drawn ligatures.

name: National
fact: It was Klim's breakout release and was praised for its quirky, warm details.

name: Poynter Oldstyle
fact: It was designed for newspaper text as part of Font Bureau's readability research.

name: Lithos
fact: It was inspired by ancient Greek inscriptions and became hugely popular on 1990s restaurant menus and posters.

name: Input
fact: It was designed for code and you can customise it before download. It even offers proportional versions for programming.

name: Cronos
fact: Slimbach based it on his own broad-pen calligraphy.

name: Méridien
fact: It was one of Frutiger's first big type designs, released the same year as Univers.

name: Espy Sans
fact: This was the system font of the Apple Newton, Apple's early handheld.

name: Goudy Old Style
fact: Goudy was astonishingly prolific and designed over 100 typefaces in his lifetime.

name: Lucida Grande
fact: It was the macOS interface font from Mac OS X until 2014, when Yosemite switched to Helvetica Neue.

name: Airbnb Cereal
fact: Airbnb created it so its product and brand would share one consistent voice.

name: Museo
fact: Buivenga made some weights free, which helped make his foundry exljbris famous.

name: Standard (Akzidenz Medium)
fact: Unimark's 1970 New York subway signage manual specified Akzidenz-Grotesk, called "Standard" in the U.S., before Helvetica took over.

name: Tekton
fact: It is based on the architectural lettering of Francis D. K. Ching, the author of architecture textbooks.

name: Perpetua
fact: It is named after Saint Perpetua, an early Christian martyr. Its companion italic was called Felicity, after her fellow martyr.

name: Cheltenham
fact: The New York Times uses Cheltenham for its headlines.

name: Zapf Chancery
fact: As one of the core fonts built into PostScript printers, it turned up on countless certificates.

name: Windsor
fact: Its heavy, cozy letterforms open the credits of many of Woody Allen's films.

name: ITC Garamond
fact: A condensed version, "Apple Garamond," served as Apple's corporate typeface from 1984 into the early 2000s.

name: Caslon
fact: The first printed copies of the U.S. Declaration of Independence, the Dunlap broadsides, are usually identified as Caslon.

name: OpenDyslexic
fact: Its letters have heavier bottoms, meant to help some dyslexic readers keep letters from seeming to flip or rotate.

name: Quadraat
fact: Smeijers drew on his study of 16th-century punchcutting.

name: Metro
fact: Dwiggins criticised existing sans serifs in his 1928 book "Layout in Advertising." Mergenthaler Linotype then challenged him to design a better one, and Metro was the result.

name: Melior
fact: Zapf based it on a "super-ellipse," a rounded-rectangle shape, which gives it a sturdy newspaper feel.

name: STIX Two
fact: A consortium of scientific publishers funded STIX to cover every mathematical symbol they needed.

name: Oakland
fact: One of Emigre's first fonts, built pixel by pixel on the original Macintosh.

name: Overpass
fact: Red Hat commissioned it as a free typeface based on U.S. Highway Gothic.

name: Neue Haas Grotesk
fact: This digital revival restores details of the original 1957 metal version that were lost in later Helvetica releases.

name: Jenson
fact: Jenson's roman, cut in Venice, is one of the earliest and most admired roman types. It still influences book typefaces today.

name: Source Serif
fact: It was inspired by the 18th-century types of Pierre-Simon Fournier and designed to pair with Source Sans.

name: Clearview
fact: The U.S. approved it for highway signs in 2004, withdrew approval in 2016, and reinstated it in 2018.

name: Lucida Console
fact: It was long the default font of the Windows command prompt.

name: ITC Bookman
fact: Its swash alternates became a signature of 1970s headlines.

name: Curlz
fact: It shipped with Microsoft Office and became a staple of birthday party invitations.

name: Glaser Stencil
fact: It comes from the designer behind "I ♥ NY" and the Bob Dylan psychedelic poster.

name: Compacta
fact: This extremely tight, dark face was a favourite of 1960s and 70s posters.

name: Warnock
fact: It is named after John Warnock, Adobe's co-founder, and was made to honour him.

name: Dom Casual
fact: It captures quick sign-painter brush lettering and was everywhere on mid-century American signage.

name: Fira Code
fact: It adds programming ligatures, so symbols like -> and != render as single glyphs.

name: Sassoon
fact: It was designed for children learning to read and write. Letters have little exit strokes that lead into joined-up handwriting.

name: Gill Sans Nova
fact: Monotype's expanded Gill Sans added dozens of styles, including some based on Gill's original drawings.

name: Times New Roman
fact: It was commissioned by The Times of London. The paper itself stopped using it in 1972.

name: Romulus
fact: Van Krimpen planned it as a huge family with sans and script companions, an early idea of a superfamily.

name: Microgramma
fact: The capitals-only predecessor of Eurostile. It has appeared in countless films and on sci-fi control panels.

name: Matrix
fact: Licko designed early Emigre fonts to work within the limits of the first Macintosh's low-resolution screens and printers.

name: Impact
fact: Released as a sturdy headline face, it was reborn online as the classic white-with-black-outline meme font.

name: Interstate
fact: Frere-Jones based it on the U.S. highway signage alphabets, turning road lettering into a typeface for print.

name: Elizabeth
fact: Friedlander designed it for the Bauer foundry. It was among the first 20th-century typefaces named after a woman designer.

name: Futura
fact: The plaque Apollo 11 left on the Moon ("Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon...") is set in Futura.

name: Rail Alphabet
fact: It was made for British Rail and also ended up on hospital signage across the UK's NHS.

name: Ionic No. 5
fact: It was built for Linotype machines. Newspapers set on them sometimes printed "etaoin shrdlu," a typo from running a finger down the keyboard.

name: Frutiger Next
fact: Frutiger updated his own classic with a true italic instead of the original sloped roman.

name: Chirp
fact: Twitter's custom typeface was adapted from GT America.

name: Poppins
fact: It supports both Latin and Devanagari, the script used for Hindi and many other languages.

name: Knockout
fact: Its widths and weights are named after boxing classes, such as Flyweight, Welterweight and Heavyweight.

name: Century
designer: Linn Boyd Benton & Theodore Low De Vinne
fact: It was created for The Century Magazine, and the name stuck to the whole family that followed.

name: Fontin
fact: Its free release made Buivenga one of the first independent designers to gain wide exposure by giving fonts away.

name: Thorowgood
fact: Thorne is credited with the "fat face," with extreme contrast and huge, heavy strokes, made for loud Victorian posters.

name: Duc de Berry
fact: It captures the lettering of the medieval Book of Hours made for the Duke of Berry.

name: Aptos
fact: It became Microsoft Office's default font in 2023. While in development it was called Bierstadt.

name: Korinna
designer: H. Berthold AG (ITC version by Ed Benguiat & Vic Caruso)
fact: For decades the clues on Jeopardy! have been displayed in a version of Korinna.

name: Nobel
fact: This Dutch geometric sans was revived by Tobias Frere-Jones for Font Bureau in 1993.

name: Public Sans
fact: It is the U.S. government's open-source typeface for its websites, derived from Libre Franklin.

name: Spencerian Script
fact: The Coca-Cola logo is written in Spencerian script, a style once taught in American schools.

name: Bitstream Charter
fact: It was designed to print well on low-resolution laser printers and was later donated for free use.

name: Menlo
fact: Apple's coding font is derived from Bitstream Vera and DejaVu Sans Mono, both open-source ancestors.
